title: In-line fluorescence characterization of sodium fluorescein and application as tracer in residence time distribution analysis at elevated temperatures
author: Hug, Meury, et al.
materials: Although several fluorescent dyes are suitable for RTD characterization, their applicability in sensitive industrial contexts such as food processing and pharmaceutical manufacturing is constrained by safety requirements. Beyond toxicological considerations, the selected tracer must exhibit favorable optical detection properties under process-relevant conditions. Sutton et al [12] analyzed different fluorophores for their application of Laser-Induced Fluorescence (LIF) for thermometry in aqueous flows and highlighted the constraints by five fundamental requirements regarding the tracer and optical setup. First, the fluorescent tracer must possess high water solubility. In the case of SF, a quenching effect occurs prior to the saturation concentration being reached. Second, it must demonstrate a quantifiable temperature sensitivity across the thermal range of interest. However, if sensitivity decreases with increasing temperature, the dependence should not be too high, since precise detection becomes more difficult with lower sensitivity. Third, the dye requires sufficient photostability to withstand the excitation intensities needed for detection without significant photobleaching. Choosing a favorable dye absorption wavelength and suitable concentration, governed by the short exposure time reduces required excitation source power and thus precludes photobleaching. Fourth, there must be adequate spectral separation between the absorption and emission bands, i.e., the Stokes shift must be large enough, to facilitate signal discrimination. Finally, re-absorption of the emitted fluorescence by the solution itself (inner filter effect) must be minimized through careful path length and concentration management.

steps.title: Prepare 0.2 M PBS stock solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve 92.07 g Na₂HPO₄ and 18.24 g KH₂PO₄ in 4.00 kg ultrapure water while stirring at room temperature to obtain a 0.2 M phosphate‑buffered saline (PBS) stock solution.

steps.title: Make 0.05 M PBS working buffers
steps.instruction: Dilute the 0.2 M PBS stock with ultrapure water to prepare 0.05 M PBS working buffers of either 5 L or 15 L, adjusting the pH to 7.40 with 1 M HCl.

steps.title: Prepare 1 g·L⁻¹ SF stock solution
steps.instruction: Dissolve 100 mg sodium fluorescein (SF, CAS 518‑47‑8, Fisher Scientific) in 100 mL of the 0.05 M PBS (pH 7.40) to obtain a 1 g·L⁻¹ SF stock solution; store in a light‑protected container at room temperature.

steps.title: Prepare 0.5 mg·L⁻¹ SF working solution
steps.instruction: Dilute the 1 g·L⁻¹ SF stock with 0.05 M PBS (pH 7.40) to reach a final SF concentration of 0.5 mg·L⁻¹; keep the solution in sealed, light‑resistant containers at room temperature and use on the same day.

steps.title: Preheat measurement system
steps.instruction: Circulate deionized (DI) water through the measurement cell and heat it with the oil bath to the desired target temperature; wait until the temperature reaches a steady‑state condition.

steps.title: Switch to SF solution and stabilize signal
steps.instruction: Replace the DI water flow with the 0.5 mg·L⁻¹ SF solution; allow the spectrofluorometer signal to stabilize, indicating steady‑state fluorescence intensity, before proceeding with measurements.

steps.title: Acquire in‑line fluorescence spectra
steps.instruction: Using FL WinLab (PerkinElmer) and later processing with Spectragryph v1.2.16.1, record fluorescence spectra from 65 °C to 136 °C with the LS50B spectrofluorometer set to excitation 490 nm, emission range 505‑550 nm, scanning speed 500 nm·min⁻¹, and both excitation and emission slit widths of 5 nm; capture four individual measurements per temperature, each with an acquisition time of ~10 s; maintain a constant mass flow of 108 g·min⁻¹ (determined by collecting effluent for 30 s); store collected samples on ice for later heat‑degradation analysis.

steps.title: Cycle between DI water and SF for each temperature
steps.instruction: After each temperature measurement, switch the flow back to DI water while the oil bath heats to the next target temperature; once the new temperature reaches steady state, switch again to the SF solution and repeat the fluorescence acquisition; perform the full temperature ramp‑up and ramp‑down sequence in triplicate on three separate days.

steps.title: Collect outlet samples for heat‑degradation analysis
steps.instruction: At the end of every temperature step of each run, collect an outlet sample of the SF solution; for each sample, pipette 200 µL into four wells of a 96‑well plate; also collect an unheated SF sample to serve as a control.

steps.title: Measure sample fluorescence in microplate reader
steps.instruction: Using a microplate reader, measure the fluorescence of each well at excitation 490 nm with a 5 nm bandwidth and emission 516 nm with a 10 nm bandwidth.
